cards.front: Recall a key point about The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: The UK has an uncodified (unwritten) constitution: no single document sets out the rules of government. Instead, the constitution comes from: statutes (laws passed by Parliament), common law (judicial precedent), conventions (unwritten rules like the PM being an MP), and authoritative works (A.V. Dicey). This makes the constitution flexible but also less clear.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: Parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament is the supreme legal authority - it can make or unmake any law. No Parliament can bind its successor. However, EU membership (1973-2020) limited sovereignty; devolution has transferred some powers; and the Human Rights Act 1998 means UK courts can declare legislation incompatible with human rights.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: Devolution: the transfer of powers from Westminster to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland Act 1998: created the Scottish Parliament with powers over health, education, justice and environment (but not defence, foreign policy). Wales Act 1998/2017: Senedd Cymru has powers over health, education, some taxation. Northern Ireland Act 1998: Stormont has powers over local matters (suspended at times due to political crisis).

cards.front: Recall a key point about The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: The West Lothian Question: Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish MPs can vote on English-only matters at Westminster, but English MPs cannot vote on devolved matters. English Votes for English Laws (EVEL) was introduced in 2015 but abolished in 2021. This remains an unresolved constitutional issue.

cards.front: Recall a key point about The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: Constitutional reform debates: should the UK adopt a codified constitution (clearer rights, limits on government power) or keep the current system (flexible, pragmatic)? Should the UK become a federal state? Should the House of Lords be reformed or abolished? Should proportional representation replace First Past the Post?

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — the uk constitution & devolution?
cards.back: 1. For The UK Constitution & Devolution questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view

cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and The UK Constitution & Devolution
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
